reason: A goes through the steps in the order they happen, names a clear endpoint for each one, and covers storage and failure cases, Redis errors included, without contradicting itself; B jumps between steps (3 to 7, 4 and 5, with link at 6), never says how the password-confirm request reaches the server, and contradicts itself on writing Google's email to users.email.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the flow in tighter, consistently structured steps that point to each other ("go to step 7") and uses a smaller flowchart, while B's longer diagram labels, its out-of-order login bullets and its self-contradicting claim that bad state is "the only case that gets an error page" make it slower and less reliable to follow.

reason: B is easier to follow: the schema comes first as a plain SQL block and the state table sits before the flowchart, every failure goes to one BACK node, and the failure table has a "state changed" column; A carries the same logic but in denser chart labels, with the schema buried in a table cell and retry loops added for races.

author: sonnet
reason: A sets out the schema and the state table before the flowchart, and sends every failure to one BACK node whose messages and state changes are listed in a single table, so a newcomer follows the flow faster; B spreads the schema into a table row, puts build changes at the end, and adds re-run-once retry loops that make the flow harder to trace.

author: haiku
reason: A is easier to follow correctly: its simple linear diagram, its table of where state lives and who writes it, and its exact failure table make clear what starts each step, where the data sits and what rolls back. author: haiku
reason: A lays the pipeline out as one straight sequence: every step uses the same starts/does/keeps/on-failure format, and the flowchart places each state store inside its system, so a newcomer can follow it top to bottom. B splits the work between a scheduler and an attempt process, describes the window in a separate section after the steps, and needs extra notes to explain its compressed diagram, so it takes longer to put together even though it covers more edge cases.

reason: A defines one consistent model (winner is first in log order, a cutoff, late events) and walks each step through what starts it, where its state lives and what happens on failure, including why it is safe; B has a convoluted dedup rule, calls `events_clean` both a table and a view, and leaves several failure paths as "not specified".

author: haiku
reason: A opens with a short summary of the whole flow, including staging and finalize, and then gives the same small steps in the same form for the live path, day close and replay, plus a failure table; B covers more, but its cutoff-and-seal step, its many forward-referenced terms (cutoff, manifest, dedup offset) and its nested sub-steps make it slower to follow, even though A's double use of `events_clean` as both table and view causes some confusion.

reason: B is quicker to follow: it defines the "winner" rule up front, its diagram keeps the replay path separate, and it uses fewer cross-referenced markers, whereas A's sealed, stale, quarantine and lock objects and its looping diagram arrow make the reader keep more moving parts in mind, even though A is a little more precise about when offsets are committed.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A covers both paths in the same Starts/Does/Data/failure layout, with a cleaner diagram, fewer moving parts and almost no forward references, so a newcomer can follow it faster; Document B adds seal, stale, quarantine, lock-release and override mechanisms, refers ahead from step 3 to step 9 and buries assumptions in a long table, so the flow is heavier to absorb.

reason: B is quicker to follow: it first explains the current system and how the queue, multipart upload and lifecycle rule behave, then describes a simple flow where every attempt restarts from the beginning, while A asks the reader to keep leases, heartbeats, staleness, checkpoint resumes and recovery branches in mind at the same time.

reason: Document A is easier for a newcomer to follow, because it defines the queue and storage rules up front and then walks through a simpler flow where each step says what starts it, what it stores and what happens on failure; Document B adds leases, heartbeats, checkpoints and a state that drops back to queued, so its steps are harder to follow even with the failure table.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to follow: each step names where it runs (browser, API server, worker), the steps are small and in order with few jumps between them, and a failure table sums things up at the end, whereas A opens with a dense list of helper APIs and makes the reader track `upload_id` persistence and a `fail_export` helper that is used before it is defined.

reason: Document A defines the export table before any step uses it, gives every step the same short template, has fewer moving parts and cross-step jumps, and ends with a failure summary table; Document B introduces fields like upload_id and expires_at before its schema appears at the end, and makes the reader jump between steps 5, 7, 8 and 9 to follow the job.

author: haiku
reason: Document A gives every step the same labelled fields (what starts it, what it does, what data it keeps, what happens if it fails) and lists the atomic script's logic as numbered steps, so a newcomer can see without guessing where state lives and how failures play out; Document B covers similar ground in looser prose and leaves some points hedged, such as saying the 429 "may also carry" the rate-limit headers.

author: haiku
reason: Both documents cover the same triggers, state and failure paths, but A tells it more simply: an expiry-based window, a short set of steps that each say what starts them, and a failure table with a "Counter changed?" column, while B adds the window-index formula, the Enterprise "counted but never rejected" mode, Redis failover and eight open questions that a newcomer must sort through before the core flow is clear.

author: sonnet
reason: A is more consistent and spells out the steps: its diagram puts the key cache inside the gateway, it reads the window from the Redis clock throughout, and it gives the atomic script line by line, whereas B's helpful opening summary is undercut by a diagram that seems to put the cache in the Key Service, a window defined first by the wall clock and then by Redis TIME, and a vague 'optional' rule for headers on a 429.

author: sonnet
reason: A states the whole flow up front in a short summary, explains the atomic check and its outcomes in one place, and puts every failure case in a single table, so a newcomer gets the right picture faster; B has more correct detail (the script steps, the cache shown inside the gateway) but spreads it across overlapping terms, decisions and notes.

author: haiku
reason: B rests on one mechanism, a per-user outbox written in the same transaction and drained by the sweeper, and spells out the write path and the switch as short ordered sub-steps; A asks the reader to hold many interlocking parts at once (updated_at cursors with 10-minute and 60-second offsets, three coverage paths, tombstone sequences, separate locks, heartbeat gates) plus forward references to later steps.

author: haiku
reason: Document A builds everything on one copy rule and one outbox mechanism, and walks each step the same way (what starts it, what changes, where state lives, what happens on failure), whereas Document B asks the reader to hold many more interacting parts at once (heartbeats, in_flight counts, gates, three change-coverage paths, time-based cursors minus 60 s, two leader locks, forward and reverse sweepers) and points ahead to later steps, which makes it slower to absorb correctly.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains the mechanism once, up front, in symmetric terms: one write-mode enum, source and mirror, the same outbox and authority table in each database, and a single "where state lives" list. author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow because it gives the write path, the drainer, the switch and the rollback as numbered sub-steps, says why each step comes in that order, and splits failures into labeled cases (crash, Postgres error, lag, stop), while A packs the same mechanics into dense definitions and paragraphs (the apply rule, the order of deletes, backfill step 5) that take more effort to untangle.

author: haiku
reason: A gives every rollback step the same fixed layout (what starts it, what it does, where its data lives, what happens on failure, when it moves on), states the route for each source mode, keeps all rollout state in one rollout record, and shows the retry loops in its diagram; B has gaps a newcomer would trip on: it calls billing_mode the one source of truth yet adds a separate rollback marker, it has the old engine charge in ChargeDue before the mode switches to old_only, and its Resolve step is vague about queued charges.

author: haiku
reason: Document A lays the rollback out as one fixed sequence of steps, gives every step the same layout (what starts it, what it keeps, what happens on failure), and has a simple fail-closed rule, so a newcomer understands it sooner; Document B's routes that depend on the source mode, the choice node, the loop from Verify back to Reconcile, the charging done implicitly at Cutover and its long list of open questions take more effort to follow.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A names one actor, the rollout controller, for every transition, and one place for each piece of state, the flag versus the rollout record, and it gives a failure rule for each rollback step; Document B leaves unclear who runs the rollback steps and who enforces the gates, and it is vague about how the old engine charges while the flag still reads both or new_only.

author: sonnet
reason: B is clearer about cause and effect: one rollout controller writes the flag, starts automatic rollbacks and watches the clock, and the pending ledger entry plus the freeze check explain how in-flight charges are found; A never says who runs its timer and automatic trigger, and its "sent, no ledger row" reconcile step leaves unclear how such a charge is detected, even though A is more compact.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a short summary, a flowchart a reader can follow and eight steps, each with one trigger, and its failure table shows order status, stock, money and cart side by side; A spreads the same flow across a 50-node diagram and steps crowded with edge cases (open-order checks, watchdog polling, re-reserve on claim, LATE_SUCCESS), so a newcomer takes longer to find the main path.

author: haiku
reason: A sets out the flow in a smaller diagram and eight steps of the same shape, each saying what starts it, what it stores and what happens on failure, so a newcomer understands it quickly; B covers more edge cases (open-order checks, the retry job, the watchdog, LATE_SUCCESS, re-reserving stock) in a much denser diagram, which slows a first reading, and that outweighs A's one small slip ("Empty cart" in the diagram against "remove confirmed lines" in the text).
